cards.explanation: The answer is False. Jehoahaz did evil in the sight of the LORD, and the verse says, “he did not turn away from them.” (2 Kings 13:2) The sins came from Jeroboam son of Nebat, an earlier king, and Jehoahaz kept walking right in them. No exit taken, friends, not one.

The answer is that he seeks the favor of the LORD. The verse says, “Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD…” (2 Kings 13:4). Aram's king Hazael had been crushing Israel, and Jehoahaz, king of Israel, took it to the LORD. That's the right place to take it, friends.

The answer is that He saw how Aram oppressed Israel. The text says the LORD listened to Jehoahaz, king of Israel, “…because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel.” (2 Kings 13:4) Notice the word saw, friends. The LORD wasn't looking the other way.

The answer is deliverer. The text says, “So the LORD gave Israel a deliverer, and they escaped the power of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 13:5) It doesn't name who the deliverer is, friends. It just tells us the LORD gave one and Israel got out from under Aram.

The answer is False. After the rescue, “…they did not turn away from the sins that the house of Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, but they continued to walk in them.” (2 Kings 13:6) The Asherah pole even stayed standing in Samaria. Free from Aram, friends, and still walking in the same sins.

The answer is True. The text says Jehoahaz “…had no army left, except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers…” (2 Kings 13:7). Ten chariots is on that short list, right alongside the horsemen and the foot soldiers. The king of Aram had destroyed his army, friends.

The answer is in Samaria. “And Jehoahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria.” (2 Kings 13:9) The passage says he reigned in Samaria seventeen years. So that's where he was laid to rest too, friends. Same city for the throne and for the grave.

The answer is his son Jehoash. “And his son Jehoash reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 13:9) The crown passed from Jehoahaz to his son. Jehoahaz was the son of Jehu, and now his own son takes the throne of Israel. Father to son, friends, just like that.

The answer is that he walks in Jeroboam's sins. Jehoash “…did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit, but he walked in them.” (2 Kings 13:11) A new king, friends, but the same old road. Same road as his father.

The answer is that he weeps over Elisha. Jehoash, king of Israel, “…came down to him and wept over him…” (2 Kings 13:14). Elisha was the prophet, and he was sick with the illness he would die from. The king wept over him, friends.

The answer is True. “So the king put his hand on the bow, and Elisha put his hands on the king’s hands.” (2 Kings 13:16) The prophet's hands rested right on the king's hands as they held the bow. The king wasn't holding that bow alone, friends. After that comes the east window and the shot.

The answer is victory. Elisha declared, “This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram…” (2 Kings 13:17). He says victory twice, friends, so he means it. That arrow had just gone out the east window.

The answer is until he has put an end to them. Elisha says, “…you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them.” (2 Kings 13:17) That's a full finish, friends, not a partial one. It's a big promise.

The answer is that he is angry with the king. “But the man of God was angry with him…” (2 Kings 13:19) Then he said, “You should have struck the ground five or six times.” The king struck three times and stopped. Elisha, the man of God, was not happy about it, friends.

The answer is False. Elisha said that five or six strikes would have put an end to Aram, and then he said, “But now you will strike down Aram only three times.” (2 Kings 13:19) Three wins, friends, not a finish. The king stopped at three strikes, and Elisha says that's how many times he will strike down Aram.

The answer is tomb. “…they threw the man’s body into Elisha’s tomb.” (2 Kings 13:21) The Israelites had seen a band of raiders. Raiders in sight, friends, so the body went into that tomb. Elisha had died and been buried, and that's where the man's body landed.

The answer is True, friends, and it's one of the wildest verses around. “And as soon as his body touched the bones of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet.” (2 Kings 13:21) The man who was thrown in there stood up. That's a burial that ended with a man on his feet.

The answer is His covenant with Israel's forefathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The text says the LORD “…turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” (2 Kings 13:23) The reason the text gives, friends, is the LORD's covenant. That covenant goes back to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The answer is the cities Hazael took from Jehoahaz. “Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Hazael had taken in battle from his father Jehoahaz.” (2 Kings 13:25) Ben-hadad was Hazael's son, and he took the throne when Hazael died. Jehoash got back what his father had lost, friends. He won three times, and the cities of Israel came home.
